I was in Agartala when the skies broke in August 2024. What followed was not a flood in the conventional sense — it was an inundation that our state had not seen since 1993. As someone who works every day with the soil of Tripura — its chemistry, its health, its future — watching 1.60 lakh hectares of farmland go underwater was not just a news event. It was a warning about what was coming after the water receded.

This piece is not about the flood itself. It is about what the flood left behind — in the soil, in the fields, in the lives of 2.66 lakh farming families — and why the story the recovery statistics don't capture may be more consequential than the damage figures themselves.

· · ·
01The Event

Tripura's Worst Flood in Three Decades

182mm
Rainfall — West Tripura, single day 21 Aug 2024

Beginning on 18 August 2024, Tripura received unprecedented monsoon rainfall over five consecutive days. On 21 August alone, West Tripura recorded 182 mm of rainfall, Khowai 157.6 mm, and Gomati 153.1 mm — intensities that overwhelmed every drainage system, embankment, and natural watershed in the state.

The disaster claimed 32 lives, left one person missing, and displaced over 38,606 families — nearly 1,47,712 individuals — seeking refuge in 821 relief camps. The worst-affected districts were South Tripura, Gomati, Khowai, and West Tripura. In total, approximately 17 lakh people across all 8 districts were impacted.

"After 1952, 1983, and 1993, Tripura witnessed such catastrophic rains, floods and landslides for the first time in over three decades."
— Agriculture & Power Minister Ratan Lal Nath · August 2024
02The Damage

The Agricultural Devastation: By the Numbers

The scale of agricultural damage was staggering — unfolding across every segment of Tripura's farm economy simultaneously.

Farmers affected2.66 lakh households—
Agriculture sector total—₹1,284 Crore

A satellite-based geospatial study using Sentinel-1 SAR imagery found that out of 85,021 hectares of agricultural land assessed, 10,510 hectares were inundated, with Gomati and West Tripura facing the greatest challenges — where 13% of total farmland was flooded.

The aid gap: Government support reached less than half of the affected farming households. Even five months later, a quarter of households continued to struggle to restore their livelihoods. (Source: Malakar & Baidya, EPRA Journals, 2025)

03The Hidden Crisis

What the Flood Left in the Soil

The financial figures, catastrophic as they are, capture only the visible and immediate loss. What they do not capture is the structural, long-term damage to Tripura's soil — damage that will suppress agricultural productivity for seasons and years after the floodwaters are long gone.

Topsoil Erosion — The Irreversible Loss

When floodwater moves at velocity across sloped agricultural land, it disaggregates and carries away the topsoil layer. Topsoil is the most nutrient-dense, biologically active layer of the soil profile. It takes between 200 and 500 years to form naturally. A single flood event can strip years of this accumulated layer in hours. Post-flood surveys documented fields covered with mud, debris, and foreign sediment — the fertile topsoil that once lay there, gone.

With landslides at over 2,500 locations, hillside farms where tribal communities practise jhum cultivation were particularly devastated. Landslides do not merely damage crops — they physically remove the farmland itself. Approximately 4,000 hectares of jhum cultivation was directly destroyed by slides like the one pictured here.

Nutrient Depletion Through Waterlogging

Extended submersion creates anaerobic conditions that destroy aerobic soil microbes — the organisms responsible for releasing nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium to plant roots. Tripura's soils — over 95% of which are already acidic with pH below 6.5 — lost significant quantities of calcium, magnesium, and potassium to leaching during the five-day inundation. Replenishment through chemical fertilisers costs hundreds of crores annually — costs that small and marginal farmers cannot absorb.

Soil Organic Carbon Depletion

Soil organic carbon (SOC) is the foundation of agricultural productivity. Tripura's soils already had critically low SOC. Flood erosion physically removes topsoil and organic matter; waterlogging accelerates anaerobic decomposition of remaining material. A soil depleted of organic carbon becomes structurally weak, nutrient-poor, and progressively less productive — regardless of how much chemical fertiliser is applied.

04Recovery Struggle

What Tripura's Farmers Faced After the Water Receded

The flood's impact disrupted food production and supply chains across the state. Floods not only affected agricultural lands and crops, but also livelihoods — for farmers and daily wage earners alike.

Post-flood recovery challenges documented in the field

  • Seed loss — stored seeds submerged; replanting impossible without external support
  • Irrigation destruction — pump houses, canals, and channels damaged; water inaccessible
  • Input cost escalation — damaged soil required higher fertiliser doses for the same yield
  • Crop cycle disruption — Aman paddy decimated mid-cycle with no time to replant
  • Debt accumulation — farmers relied on informal borrowing and temporary migration
  • Livestock loss — 1,454 cattle removed both farm power and financial collateral

Field research by Dr. Rajib Malakar and Shri Joyjit Baidya (EPRA Journals, 2025) confirms that nearly 90% of surveyed households reported significant income losses, with small and marginal farmers bearing disproportionately heavy burdens.

05Root Causes

Why the Floods Hit So Hard

Pre-existing Soil Fragility

Tripura's soils entered the 2024 monsoon season already severely stressed. Decades of intensive chemical fertiliser use, declining organic matter, chronic acid pH, and annual erosion had left agricultural soils with minimal structural resilience. When the flood came, there was no buffer.

Deforestation and Climate Change

Deforestation and unplanned development have progressively intensified Tripura's flood vulnerability. The 2024 floods were widely characterised by environmental experts as a direct manifestation of climate-change-intensified extreme weather. As global temperatures rise, such events are projected to become dramatically more frequent — making soil resilience a permanent challenge, not a one-time recovery problem.

The Path Forward: Building Soil That Survives the Next Flood

The most effective, locally available tool for building soil resilience is one that Tripura's own forests have been producing for centuries: biochar. 06Closing

2024 Was a Warning. Are We Building Soil That Can Answer It?

The official loss figure for Tripura's agriculture from the August 2024 floods is ₹1,284 crore. These numbers capture the visible, immediate loss — the submerged paddy, the swept-away vegetables, the dead livestock.

What they do not capture is the compounding, invisible damage: the topsoil now in the Gomati River, on its way to the Bay of Bengal. The organic carbon that will take decades to rebuild. The acid soils that are slightly more acid. The structural resilience that was slightly weaker when the 2025 monsoon arrived.

Flood damage is measured in one season. Soil damage compounds across many seasons.

We can rebuild a house in months. We cannot rebuild topsoil in years. The 2024 floods were not just a humanitarian disaster — they were a soil health emergency that will quietly suppress agricultural productivity long after the relief camps have closed.
— Er. Debasis Das · CEO & Co-Founder, Trichar · Agartala, Tripura

At Trichar, the 2024 floods strengthened our conviction that building soil resilience through biochar is not an agricultural nicety — it is a climate adaptation imperative for every farming community in Northeast India.
